samples.summary: Quadratic backtracking (ReDoS) in `IMG_TAG_RE` — a stored note can freeze every collaborator's preview
samples.evidence:
`const IMG_TAG_RE = /^<img(\s[^<>]*?)?\s*\/?>/i;` (img-plugin.ts:53) has two quantifiers that both match whitespace and are adjacent: the lazy `[^<>]*?` inside the optional group, and the greedy `\s*` that follows it. On an input that starts with `<img` and never closes, the engine tries every split of the whitespace run between the two quantifiers, and for each split backtracks `\s*` position by position looking for `>`; total work is O(n^2) in the length of the whitespace run.

Attack: a workspace member (notes are collaborative — see the stored-XSS SECURITY note at preview.ts:188) stores a note containing a single paragraph

    <img<SPACE repeated 200_000 times>x

(no `<` or `>` after it, and a trailing non-space so the paragraph trim does not remove the run). markdown-it's inline `text` rule treats `<` as a terminator, so `imgRule` runs at that position (img-plugin.ts:130), `startsImgTag` passes, and `IMG_TAG_RE.exec` at img-plugin.ts:132 enters ~2e10 backtracking steps on the main thread. `NotePreview.render()` calls `md.render()` synchronously into `this.el.innerHTML` (preview.ts:346) and is invoked on every document change, so the reader's tab hangs and — because the editor pane renders the same preview — is hard to recover from without deleting the note out of band.

This is not pre-existing behaviour: with `html: false` the `html_inline` rule is inert, and markdown-it's own `autolink` rule bails on this input after a single `indexOf('>')`. The new regex introduces the blowup. A possessive/atomic shape (e.g. dropping the inner `\s*` and letting `[^<>]*` be greedy, or requiring `>` via a cheap `indexOf` pre-check before running the regex) removes it.

samples.summary: `width`/`height` allow `0`/`1`, turning any note into an invisible tracking beacon the repo's own threat model calls out
samples.evidence: `DIMENSION_RE = /^\d+%?$/` (img-plugin.ts:63) accepts `0` and `1`, and the emitted token carries whatever the author wrote (img-plugin.ts:155-156). `mermaid.ts:58-61` states this repo's position explicitly: an attacker-controlled image fetch in a note discloses "every reader's IP, User-Agent, and reading time to the note's author", and mermaid.ts:92 records that the repo has no CSP. `md.validateLink` gates only the scheme, not the origin, so `` is accepted verbatim. The fetch itself is pre-existing (`![](https://attacker/x.png)` already does it), so this is an amplification rather than a new class: the sizing attributes let the beacon be rendered at 1x1 (or 0) so the reader has no visual cue that a remote resource was loaded, where an intrinsic-size render usually gives one. Worth a deliberate decision (clamp to a minimum, or land the `img-src` CSP mermaid.ts:92 already recommends) rather than an accident.

samples.summary: Scheme-rejection tests cover only a literal `javascript:` — no case for entity-encoded or whitespace-prefixed schemes, which is exactly where the unescape-then-validate order could go wrong
samples.evidence: `parseAttrs` runs `md.utils.unescapeAll` on the raw attribute value (img-plugin.ts:105) BEFORE `normalizeLink`/`validateLink` (img-plugin.ts:143-144). That ordering is what makes `` and `` safe, and it is the single most load-bearing security property of this plugin. The refusal table (img-plugin.test.ts:83) asserts only the literal `['a javascript: url', '']`. Nothing pins the encoded, whitespace-prefixed, control-character-prefixed, or `data:image/svg+xml` variants, so a future refactor that moves `unescapeAll` after `validateLink` (or drops it) would keep the whole suite green while opening a real XSS. I traced the current code and believe it is safe today; the gap is that nothing holds it there.
searchedFor: read packages/notes/src/view/img-plugin.test.ts in full (all 17 refusal cases + 11 acceptance cases)
grep for validateLink/normalizeLink across the repo

samples.summary: `state.src.slice(state.pos, state.posMax)` runs once per `<img` occurrence, giving an O(n·k) path a note can control
samples.evidence: img-plugin.ts:132 slices the remaining inline chunk for every position where `startsImgTag` matches, so a note body of `<img` repeated k times slices k times. The header comment at img-plugin.ts:113-118 says the charCode pre-check exists so "slicing the rest of the chunk each time would be quadratic" — but the slice still happens on the matching path. In practice V8 returns a SlicedString in O(1) and `RegExp` can read it via a flat-content pointer into the parent, so this is likely not exploitable on its own; I could not construct a hang from it separately from the `IMG_TAG_RE` finding above. Recording it because it compounds that finding and because the comment reads as if the cost were avoided.

verdict.reason: The regex is present verbatim at img-plugin.ts:53 (`/^<img(\s[^<>]*?)?\s*\/?>/i`) and its two adjacent whitespace-matching quantifiers (lazy `[^<>]*?` then greedy `\s*`) do produce O(n^2) backtracking on `<img` + long whitespace run with no closing `>`: for each lazy expansion the greedy `\s*` consumes the remainder and backtracks position-by-position hunting `\/?>`. The cheap pre-filter at img-plugin.ts:120-127 only compares the 4 chars `<img`, so it does not bound the pathological input, and there is no `indexOf('>')` or length cap before `IMG_TAG_RE.exec(state.src.slice(state.pos, state.posMax))` at img-plugin.ts:132. Reachability holds: `md.use(imgPlugin)` at preview.ts:83 registers the rule before `html_inline` (img-plugin.ts:177), so `html: false` does not neutralize it; `NotePreview.render()` calls `md.render()` synchronously into innerHTML at preview.ts:346 and editor.ts:294 re-renders the whole document on every change. I searched packages/notes/src for any truncation/size guard on note content and found none (only display-name.ts:55 caps an unrelated field). Note content is collaborator-supplied and stored — the same threat model the preview's own SECURITY comment at preview.ts:187-193 acknowledges — so a stored note freezes other members' tabs. Untrusted input driving unbounded regex work is in the security lane (unsafe input handling, CWE-1333) with an availability impact, consistent with the reported major severity. No named refutation ground applies: the code is present as described, no guard makes it unreachable, and I found no counterexample to the quadratic shape.
